title: A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States
lead: Federal recovery codes made local poultry practices criminal offenses. The Schechter businesses challenged both the breadth of presidential code-making and Congress’s power over the Brooklyn transactions being prosecuted.

actors.name: A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corporation, Schechter Live Poultry Market, and the Schechter brothers
actors.role: Brooklyn slaughterhouse businesses and their individual operators; criminal defendants.

actors.name: The President
actors.role: Approved the metropolitan New York Live Poultry Code under NIRA § 3.

actors.name: Industry associations
actors.role: Proposed code provisions; their expertise and representativeness became part of the delegation debate.

actors.name: United States
actors.role: Prosecuted code violations and sought reinstatement of wage-and-hour convictions on appeal.

proceedings: Of sixty indictment counts, the trial court dismissed twenty-seven and defendants were acquitted on fourteen; they were convicted on eighteen substantive counts and one conspiracy count.
Second Circuit affirmed conspiracy and sixteen substantive convictions but reversed two wage-and-hour convictions.
Supreme Court on May 27, 1935 reversed the sustained convictions and left the wage-and-hour reversals intact; no Justice dissented.
limits: The Court resolved delegation and its then-applicable commerce analysis, leaving Fifth Amendment objections undecided. The commerce discussion describes the 1935 holding rather than a present-day test. It did not find the challenged practices harmless or beyond state regulation.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress authorizes industrial codes with criminal consequences
sections.cue: Which choices did the statute leave to industry and the President?
paragraphs: The Schechter brothers bought poultry for local slaughter and sale through two Brooklyn businesses, A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corporation and Schechter Live Poultry Market. Their practices became subject to a federal industrial-code system. Section 3 of the National Industrial Recovery Act allowed the President to approve fair-competition codes proposed by representative trade or industry groups. He had to find no inequitable membership restrictions, no promotion of monopolies or oppression of small enterprises, and a tendency to advance statutory policy. He could attach conditions, exceptions, and exemptions or prescribe a code if none had been approved.

The policy embraced industrial rehabilitation, greater purchasing power, reduced unemployment, better labor standards, fuller productive capacity, and elimination of unfair competition. A violation in a transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce was a misdemeanor carrying a fine up to $500, with each additional day potentially a separate offense. Congress thus supplied penalties while leaving the content of numerous binding industrial rules to the code process.

On April 13, 1934, the President approved the metropolitan New York Live Poultry Code. It regulated hours, wages, labor relations, staffing, trade practices, administration, records, and reports. Subject to exceptions, it limited work to forty hours a week and required fifty cents an hour; it also prohibited employment under sixteen. Industry associations proposed rules but were neither the prosecuting government nor a legislature. The rules’ penal force ultimately depended on presidential action.

sections.title: The Schechters buy interstate poultry for local slaughter and sale
sections.cue: What conduct produced the criminal convictions?
paragraphs: A. L. A. Schechter Poultry Corporation and Schechter Live Poultry Market operated Brooklyn slaughterhouse markets through the Schechter brothers. They bought poultry largely brought from other states, transported it to their premises, and slaughtered or sold it to local dealers and butchers supplying consumers. Once bought for this local disposition, the birds were not intended to resume interstate travel.

One code rule required purchase by coop or half-coop instead of selection of individual birds. Ten counts charged the defendants with permitting individual selection. Other convictions concerned wages and hours, an unfit chicken, inspections, licensing, and reports. The case therefore concerned concrete criminal enforcement against local practices rather than abstract review of a recovery policy.

The federal indictment contained sixty counts. Twenty-seven were dismissed, fourteen produced acquittals, and eighteen substantive counts plus a conspiracy count produced convictions. The Second Circuit upheld conspiracy and sixteen substantive convictions but reversed two wage-and-hour convictions. Both sides obtained Supreme Court review of their losses: defendants attacked surviving convictions, and the government sought restoration of the wage-and-hour convictions.

sources.pinpoint: Parties, material facts, procedural history; 295 U.S. at 519–21 & n.2, 527–28, 542–43, 550

sections.title: Hughes asks whether Congress made the governing policy choices
sections.cue: Why did an emergency and broad recovery objectives fail to suffice?
paragraphs: After argument on May 2–3, 1935, Chief Justice Hughes addressed defendants’ delegation and commerce objections. Defendants also raised Fifth Amendment issues. Economic emergency explained the Act but could not enlarge assigned constitutional powers. Congress needed flexibility because it could not legislate every administrative detail. The problem was therefore not discretion itself, but whether Congress first supplied governing policies and standards before entrusting subordinate rules or factual decisions to administrators.

“Fair competition” did not identify an adequately bounded existing body of law. Common-law unfair competition chiefly concerned deceptive appropriation of another trader’s business or goods and related wrongs. These codes reached wages, hours, and affirmative industrial planning far beyond that domain. The government did not claim that only previously unlawful conduct could be prohibited. A general label of industrial betterment left central legislative choices to code makers.

The comparison to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) also failed. Under the FTC Act, an expert agency addressed particular unfair-method allegations through complaints, evidence, findings, and judicial review. Those mechanisms linked judgment to legal standards and concrete disputes. The recovery scheme had broader substantive reach without comparable constraint. Hughes did not hold that all delegations must use adjudication; his comparison concerned the combined scope and safeguards.

sections.title: Representativeness and presidential approval leave the central choices open
sections.cue: How did this scheme differ from accepted administrative delegations?
paragraphs: Industry knowledge could assist government, Hughes reasoned, but expertise did not confer lawmaking power. Requiring a representative association identified who could propose rules without determining what they could command. Anti-monopoly and small-business protections left a vast range of production, marketing, wage, and other policy choices untouched.

The required presidential finding that a code promoted statutory policy offered little more: the aims were broad enough to encompass almost any recovery program. The President could modify proposals, supply exceptions, or write a code himself; assisting officials’ reports did not bind him. Congress had not furnished a workable standard separating authorized choices from unauthorized ones across all these industries.

Earlier cases involved more bounded tasks. Common-carrier legislation established a framework applied to transportation evidence. Radio licensing concerned a limited resource and service standards. Hampton tied tariff adjustments to differences in production costs. Hughes preserved those precedents while refusing to extend them to unrestricted industrial-code creation. The comparison with Aurora, Field, and Grimaud likewise concerned what Congress had already specified—conditions and consequences or management purposes—not a demand that administration be mechanical.

sources.pinpoint: Delegation reasoning and notes; 295 U.S. at 537–42

sections.title: The birds’ interstate journey has ended
sections.cue: Why did the Court separately reject the commerce basis?
paragraphs: The commerce inquiry concerned these birds and transactions. Their earlier shipment from other states did not make every later sale interstate forever. At the Brooklyn premises they were held for local sale and consumption with no planned interstate continuation. Cases involving temporary stops within a continuing stream did not fit.

The government also argued that low wages and long hours reduced costs, depressed poultry prices, and damaged the interstate price structure. Under the Court’s then-used direct/indirect distinction, that chain was too remote. Accepting it would authorize control over rent, advertising, staffing, and nearly every local business expense. The Court distinguished conduct directly obstructing interstate transportation or deliberately restraining interstate trade; defendants had been prosecuted for code violations, not such a separate restraint.

The same reasoning covered selection of chickens, the unfit bird, and local reporting, licensing, and inspections. The Court did not declare those practices harmless or immunize them from state regulation. It rejected this federal code’s reach on the particular commerce theory. This historical reasoning is distinct from a claim about the test governing modern disputes.

sections.title: Cardozo distinguishes bounded choices from industrial lawmaking
sections.cue: What did his concurrence add about inseparability?
paragraphs: Justice Cardozo, joined by Justice Stone, concurred. He contrasted this statute with the narrower delegation he had defended in his Panama Refining dissent: there executive discretion concerned when to take a specified action; here it included discovering industrial problems and choosing broad regulatory solutions without even an approximate standard.

Cardozo accepted identifying and prohibiting unfair practices under established standards, with industry consultation. He objected when code makers could order whatever affirmative improvements they thought would advance prosperity. Prohibiting selective chicken buying illustrated the difference: it displaced an established practice without grounding the prohibition in a preexisting ethical or commercial norm. Even a narrowing construction would leave the code so pervasively beyond authorization that separating valid provisions would destroy the arrangement.

He also agreed on commerce. Remote economic repercussions did not nationalize local transactions, and degree mattered. Wages and hours were integral to the code plan, so excising those provisions would not preserve a workable remainder. His concurrence thus addressed both breadth of delegated choice and the inseparability of the regulatory components.

sections.title: The challenged criminal rules cannot support convictions
sections.cue: What happened to each side’s appeal?
paragraphs: On May 27, 1935, the unanimous Court reversed the portion of the Second Circuit judgment sustaining convictions and left intact its reversal of the wage-and-hour convictions challenged by the government. The legal authorization supporting the challenged criminal rules was invalid; the Court did not merely require a better presidential explanation or send defendants back for another decision under the same code.

The delegation and commerce grounds independently defeated the convictions, leaving the Fifth Amendment objections unnecessary to decide. More precise legislative instructions might cure delegation without establishing commerce power over a transaction; an adequate interstate connection would not supply missing legislative standards. No Justice dissented. The full opinion’s commerce discussion and Cardozo concurrence supplement the assigned excerpt’s principal focus on delegation.
